newsitem.title: UK: Sicily borrows cheaper money via securitised bond.
newsitem.headline: Sicily borrows cheaper money via securitised bond.

text.p: The Italian city of Sicily has borrowed 1.7 trillion lire ($1.0 billion) from Credit Suisse First Boston in a cost-effective transaction involving securitisation, CSFB said on Monday.
"CSFB London branch won the Sicily loan in a competitive tender a month or so ago," Anthony Faulkner, director of private placements at CSFB, told Reuters.
"We added to that a swap from Credit Suisse Financial Products, and via special purpose vehicle Rossini generated $1.0 billion of amortising FRNs," he said.
Rossini, a Dutch special purpose vehicle which is an acronym for Repackaged Obligations of Sicily Structured Into Note Issue, launched a $1.0 billion floating-rate note on Monday.
The dollar deal matures in February 2008, pays 45 basis points over six-month Libor and is secured on a 1.7 trillion lire loan to Sicily.
"We won the mandate for the underlying loan against Italian domestic banks," Faulkner said.

"We have taken what was an Italian domestic transaction and transformed it into an international capital markets transaction," he said, adding CSFB was able to undercut Italian banks bidding for the deal by structuring the issue.
Sicily will receive the funds on the same day as the payment date of the FRN, June 13.
CSFB is in negotiations with an insurance agency to obtain cover for up to half the bond, which would effectively make the risk on the insured paper AAA.
The rest of the paper has an implied A minus credit rating, Faulkner said.
"The deal is seen as a 20 percent risk-weighted asset in most jurisdictions, has an A minus implied rating and a coupon of Libor plus 45 b.p.," Faulkner said.

"This is attractive under current market conditions. We are also finalising negotiations with an insurance agency to guarantee 1/4 to 1/2 of the bonds. The bond plus the insurance policy means investors can allocate it against AAA lines," he said.
"That enables us to approach two investor bases."

European municipalities are increasingly tapping the international capital markets to raise funds. CSFB underwrote a similar securitised deal for Portuguese railways, and other borrowers have come to the market.

"With European economic and monetary union (EMU) looming, central governments are increasingly keen that sub-sovereign entities finance themselves rather than come running to the state," Faulkner said.
Although Sicily was able to tap dollar-based FRN investors, the structure means its exposure remains in fixed-rate Italian lira.
-- Aline van Duyn, London newsroom +44 171 542 7748 ($ = 1695 Italian Lire)
